boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Scharnitz entry (4 November 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Marshal Ney's attack on the Tyrolean pass of Scharnitz, held by Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne. The frame has no separate entry for the Leutasch work, which General Loison's column turned and took the same day, so this draft covers it, and the surrender of Swinburne's column near Seefeld after it left the fortress in the night, which both other accounts tell as the end of the action and Victoires dates to 5 November. Ney's march from Ulm, the Innsbruck defence deputation's measures, the French entry into Innsbruck and Archduke John's withdrawal to the Brenner are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) about 13,000 men under Marshal Ney and side B (Austrian) about 3,000 men under Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Neither figure is in the passages read. Moriggl gives side B's regulars as 944 men at Scharnitz and a battalion given as 600 at the Leutasch work, with about 900 Landesvertheidiger at Scharnitz and militia companies of 117 and 219 at the Leutasch (claims moriggl-scharnitz and moriggl-leutasch): 2,780 together (our sum, not a source's total). The passages read do not show whether Bodart's 3,000 counts both posts or the Landesvertheidiger. Neither other account gives side A a total for the action; Moriggl gives Labassée's brigade, sent against the Leutasch, as 3000 men (claim moriggl-side-a), and his order of battle at the Rhine crossing gives Ney's corps 24,267 men, Loison's division 8014 and Malcher's 7601 (claim moriggl-order-of-battle). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French (about 13,000 men) under Marshal Ney over the Austrians (about 3,000 men) under Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian) at Scharnitz, the Tyrolean account's figures: Moriggl lists the forces the commandant had at his disposal as 1 battalion of the infantry regiment Erzherzog Ludwig under Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne, 558 men; 1 weak battalion of the regiment Erzherzog Karl, 295; artillerymen, 71; staff dragoons, 20; together 944 men, with only 12 guns in the fortress. Seven companies of Landesvertheidiger stood in support: four militia companies, 594 men by a strength return before him; Anton Grueber of Seefeld's volunteer rifle company of 93 men, at Scharnitz since 13 October; and two rifle companies that arrived on 4 November, which he takes as 213 men, so that the Landesvertheidiger present at the assault numbered about 900.
claims.rationale: Side B's own side's figures (Moriggl writes the Tyrolean account), read from the page images. The population is the forces 'the commandant had at his disposal' and, for the Landesvertheidiger, those present at the assault. Moriggl takes the 594 from a strength return and the 213 as his own assumption; he gives no source for the 944. In his OCR the Erzherzog Karl battalion was sent from Innsbruck by the army command with guns, and Swinburne reported that guns and battalion had arrived; the passages read do not say whether the 12 guns include those sent. The garrison and its reinforcement were in place before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited; Leiß, not Swinburne, drew the two rifle companies to Scharnitz. English renderings (ours): 'of 1 battalion of the infantry regiment Erzherzog Ludwig under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne'; 'strength of the battalion | 558 men'; 'further of 1 weak battalion of the regiment Erzherzog Karl; its strength | 295 [men]'; 'artillerymen | 71 [men]'; 'staff dragoons | 20 [men]'; 'together | 944 men'; 'there were only 12 guns in the fortress, when one could easily have needed and used 50'; 'in support of the military there stood in that area the following 7 companies of Landesvertheidiger'; 'these four militia companies numbered 594 men by a strength return before [me]'; 'to these come three rifle companies, namely Anton Grueber of Seefeld's volunteer rifle company of 93 men, standing at Scharnitz since 13 October'; 'then the two rifle companies that arrived on 4 November (from where? and led by whom? unknown) at the same time as the Hörtenberg Landsturm in the place just named, and were drawn to Scharnitz by the rifle major Herr von Leiß'; 'if we take these two companies at 213 men, the number of all Landesvertheidiger present at the assault on the fortress comes to about 900'; 'to this end a battalion of the regiment Erzherzog Karl was quickly set in motion from Innsbruck by the army command to reinforce the garrison of Scharnitz; at the same time ... (OCR) guns were sent there' (OCR); 'Swinburne reported that he had duly received the Archduke's orders through engineer captain Peschke, that the guns and the battalion Erzherzog Karl had also already arrived; that he had now occupied all the works' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B (Austrian) at the Leutasch work, the Tyrolean account's figures: on 4 November a battalion of the infantry regiment Franz Kinsky, whose strength is given as 600 men, held the work under Major Kraus, commander of the battalion and the fort, and three guns and a howitzer armed it. Two militia companies were in the Leutasch: one from the court district of Hörtenberg, 117 men under Captain Franz Sailer, and one from Petersberg, 219 men under Joseph Marberger. Moriggl says Kraus had 900 men at his disposal and posted 24 soldiers with an officer on the Alpl and 14 militiamen under a corporal on the Grünkopf; on 4 November the usual 38 men stood on those posts.
claims.rationale: Side B's own side's figures, read from the page images. Moriggl says the battalion's 600 'is given' without naming who gives it; his 900 at Kraus's disposal is close to 600, 117 and 219 together (936, our sum). The garrison was in place before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited; the posts on the Alpl and the Grünkopf were Kraus's own dispositions (claim leutasch-command). The Landsturm columns that came up during the fight are not counted: Moriggl gives the first, under Anton Seeger, a strength seen only in the OCR, and none for the other two. English renderings (ours): 'on 4 November there was in the Leutasch work, as already mentioned, a battalion of the infantry regiment Franz Kinsky, whose strength is given as 600 men'; 'commander of the said battalion and of the fort was Major Kraus'; 'three guns and a howitzer formed the armament of the place'; 'one of them was from the former court district of Hörtenberg (now Telfs), numbered 117 men and stood under Captain Franz Sailer'; 'the other was from the court district of Petersberg (Silz), was 219 men strong and was commanded by Joseph Marberger, son of the Pfleger of Silz'; 'but Major Kraus did none of all this, although he had 7 days' time and 900 men at his disposal; he was content to order 24 men of the military with an officer up to the Alpl, and 14 men of the militia under a corporal up to the Grünkopf, and that was that'; 'on this day the usual 38 men again stood up on the said posts'; 'the first column of Landsturm men that came up was about ... (OCR) men strong and stood under the command of Anton Seeger' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B (Austrian), side A's account: Victoires says the Leutasch, a fortified post that Loison's division invested, was defended by three hundred men, who capitulated; in the fort of Scharnitz the 69th regiment found only about a hundred Tyrolean chasseurs and some inhabitants, the rest of the troops having decided to evacuate the place and retire on Innsbruck. It gives no total for side B.
claims.rationale: Side A's history on side B, read from the page images; it names no source in the passages read. Its three hundred at the Leutasch are far fewer than Moriggl's battalion given as 600 with two militia companies (claim moriggl-leutasch). Its hundred chasseurs in the fort do not fit Moriggl's account, in which the Landesvertheidiger were told to find their own way out and Ney entered an abandoned fortress (claims side-b-command and side-a-command). The eighteen hundred men it gives as taken are recorded as a loss (claim side-b-losses-reported). English renderings (ours): 'General Loison's division invested this fortified post, made the three hundred men who defended it capitulate, and then marched on Seefeld, a village lying in front of the Pass of Scharnitz, which the marshal wanted to attack'; as in claim scharnitz-ground for the sixty-ninth's escalade; 'they found in the fort only about a hundred Tyrolean chasseurs and some inhabitants; the rest of the troops had decided to evacuate the place to retire on Innsbruck'.

claims.value: Side A (French) in Moriggl: early on 4 November Marshal Ney marched out of Mittenwald with Malher's division and Marcognet's brigade, placing the infantry to the right of the road and the cavalry to the left, with the artillery on the road and part of it left in reserve in the Mühlfeld under General Serroux; he sent Labassée's brigade, 3000 men strong, under General of Division Loison from Mittenwald to turn the Leutasch work, take it and then take the fortress of Scharnitz in the rear. Loison advanced with the reinforced brigade Labassée, and at the Leutasch French officers told Captain Baron Horn that a French column of over 3000 men stood in the rear of the work. Moriggl's narrative gives no total for side A.
claims.rationale: Side B's account of side A, read from the page images except where marked OCR; Moriggl names no source for these figures. In his OCR the storming of the outworks fell to Marcognet's brigade, Roguet's brigade moved against the Teufelskuchl battery and turning columns were formed from Villatte's brigade; he also says that Ney had had to leave a considerable part of his forces at Ulm and that his division under Dupont was employed elsewhere. The troops named are those Ney committed against the two posts for this action, so the claim is tagged commander_created; the corps he had was set by orders from above (claim side-a-objectives). The passages read do not say whether the brigade's 3000 and the column of over 3000 are one figure. His order of battle at the Rhine crossing is recorded in claim moriggl-order-of-battle. English renderings (ours): 'at last the fourth of November had dawned! Early in the morning Marshal Ney marched out of Mittenwald with the division Malher and the brigade Marcognet'; 'to the right of the road he placed the infantry, to the left the cavalry; on the road itself the artillery advanced, of which a part stayed behind as reserve in the so-called Mühlfeld under the command of General Serroux'; 'the brigade Labassée, 3000 men strong, Ney sent off from Mittenwald under the command of General of Division Loison, that excellent and ever-fortunate leader of turning columns, to turn the Leutasch work, take it and then take the fortress of Scharnitz in the rear'; 'in accordance with the orders received, the French General of Division Loison advanced on 4 November with the reinforced brigade Labassée'; 'that a French column over 3000 men strong stood in the rear of the work'; '[a part of the] French infantry [went] across to take by storm the ... (OCR) "Maulecke" as well as the "Vorschanzl". This difficult task fell to the brigade Marcognet' (OCR); 'the brigade Roguet set out against the battery lying on the right side, the Teufelskuchl' (OCR); 'from the brigade Villatte ... (OCR) turning columns were formed, of which the ... (OCR) tried to push forward over the Brunnstein toward the Karwendel valley, but the ... (OCR) wanted to come into the rear of the fortress over the Arnthal' (OCR); 'at Ulm the marshal had had to leave a considerable part of his forces behind, while besides his ... (OCR) division (Dupont)' (p. 321, OCR) 'was employed elsewhere' (p. 322, OCR).

claims.value: Side A (French) in Moriggl's order of battle of the Grande Armée 'at its crossing of the Rhine': Marshal Ney's VI Army Corps had Dupont's division, 7 battalions and 5350 men; Loison's division (brigadiers Villatte and Roguet; 6th light, 39th, 69th and 76th line regiments), 9 battalions and 8014 men; Malcher's division (brigadiers Marcognet and Labassée; 25th light, 27th, 50th and 59th line), 9 battalions and 7601 men; Tilly's cavalry division (10th Chasseurs, 1st and 3rd Hussars), 12 squadrons and 2169 men; and artillerymen, engineers and others, 1168 men: in all 25 battalions, 12 squadrons and 24,267 men.
claims.rationale: Side B's account of side A, read from the page images. The sentence that introduces the table (p. 89) dates it to the army's crossing of the Rhine, which Moriggl does not date, and he names no source for it. It gives the corps at the crossing, which comes before Elchingen and Ulm in Moriggl's narrative, not side A on 4 November: in Moriggl's OCR Ney had had to leave a considerable part of his forces at Ulm, and his division under Dupont was employed elsewhere (claim moriggl-side-a). The table puts Marcognet's and Labassée's brigades in Malcher's division and Villatte's and Roguet's in Loison's; Moriggl's narrative engages all four at the two posts (claim moriggl-side-a), and the 69th regiment, which Victoires has attack the fort in front (claim victoires-side-a), is in Loison's division. Loison's and Malcher's divisions number 15,615 together at the crossing (our sum, not a source's total), against Bodart's about 13,000 for side A (claim bodart-strength); the passages read do not show Bodart's basis or how much of either division was at the two posts. The corps' composition and strength were set before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. The table prints 'Malcher' where the narrative prints 'Malher'. English renderings (ours): 'there now follow the distribution and the statement of the strength of the Grande Armée at its crossing of the Rhine'; 'VI Army Corps — Marshal Ney'; each division row gives the division's commander, its brigadiers, its regiments ('leichtes' light, 'L.-I.-R.' line infantry regiment, '„' ditto), battalions, squadrons and men; Tilly's row ('Kavallerie-Div.', cavalry division; 'Chasseur'; 'Husar.', hussars) gives 12 squadrons and 2169 men; 'artillerymen, engineers etc. | 1168'; the corps total, '25 | 12 | 24,267'.

claims.value: Side A (French), its own account: Victoires says Napoleon directed Marshal Ney with his army corps to invade the Tyrol; General Loison's division invested the Leutasch post and then marched on Seefeld; on 5 November at two in the morning Loison directed two columns on the fort of Scharnitz, one to turn it and the second, formed by the 69th regiment, to attack in front. The first column, sent to cut off the Austrians' retreat, was inferior in force when it met them near a monastery, until the 69th came up. It gives no total.
claims.rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images; it names no source in the passages read and mentions no assault on 4 November. The columns were Loison's dispositions for this action, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'Napoleon, before leaving Augsburg, had directed Marshal Ney with his army corps on Landsberg, to make an invasion of the Tyrol and seize that country'; as in claim victoires-side-b for the Leutasch; 'on 5 November, at two in the morning, General Loison directed two columns on the fort of Scharnitz, one of which was to turn this post while the second would attack in front'; 'the sixty-ninth regiment, which formed this second column, and which had so distinguished itself at the combat of Elchingen, found in its way obstacles that would have seemed insurmountable to any but such brave men'; 'in carrying out this movement the Austrians met the first column, which General Loison had directed to that side to cut off their retreat'; 'the combat began near a monastery that stood on the road; the French column, inferior in force, was on the point of leaving the passage free to its adversaries when the sixty-ninth regiment, which had just taken Scharnitz and had at once thrown itself in pursuit of the fleeing garrison, arrived on the field and changed the face of the combat'.

claims.value: Side A was Marshal Ney's corps. In Moriggl's OCR, Ney reconnoitred the fortress and the Leutasch valley with his staff and men who knew the area, had Swinburne summoned in writing through Colonel Colbert and, on his refusal, decided to take the place by force of arms. On 4 November Ney sent General Loison with Labassée's brigade to turn and take the Leutasch work and then take Scharnitz in the rear, and before acting against the fortress sent an envoy once more at 10 o'clock (Colbert again, OCR); then followed a general advance (OCR) and assaults from 1 o'clock to ¼ past 5. Loison took the Leutasch work, where Captain Dauphin was left as commandant, and advanced to Seefeld the same evening; there French detachments pushed Swinburne's column off the road, fell on its flank and forestalled it at the defile, and it surrendered. Ney, told in the night of 4 to 5 November, it was said by a deserter, that the garrison had left, set out very early and entered the abandoned fortress toward 4 in the morning. In Victoires, Loison's division invested the Leutasch, and Loison directed the two columns against Scharnitz.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as the accounts give them (page images except where marked OCR). Moriggl asks why Ney sent a turning column and then, without awaiting its result, had the fortress stormed, and inclines to parish priest Grün's view that pride alone moved him to it, to increase his glory by taking the place by force of arms (OCR); that is a judgment, not a recorded motive. English renderings (ours): 'in the forenoon of the ... (OCR) November Ney, at the head of his general staff and some men who knew the area, made a reconnaissance against the fortress and to the right against the Leutasch valley, which opens between Mittenwald and Scharnitz' (OCR); 'the French Colonel Colbert was the bearer of the letter' (OCR); 'in consequence of the refusal Ney now decided to take the place by force of arms' (OCR); as in claim moriggl-side-a for Labassée's brigade; 'but before Marshal Ney had anything undertaken against the fortress, he sent once more at 10 o'clock an envoy with a' (p. 331) '[trumpeter to Swinburne]; it was the same Colonel Colbert who the day before at the same hour had brought the marshal's letter' (p. 332, OCR); 'now followed a general advance of the enemy' (OCR); 'from 1 o'clock to ¼ past 5 o'clock, thus four full hours, the storming went on without pause'; 'in the work the French Captain Dauphin was now left behind as commandant'; 'General Loison advanced the same evening over the so-called "Böden" to Seefeld, the moonlight serving him excellently'; as in claim side-b-command for the action at Seefeld; 'for in the night of 4 to 5 November he had received at Mittenwald, as people say through a deserter, the news that the garrison of Scharnitz had already left'; 'the marshal therefore set out from Mittenwald very early and entered the completely abandoned fortress toward 4 in the morning'; 'one might rightly ask for what reason Ney sent off a turning column and, without awaiting the result of its dispatch, had the fortress stormed' (OCR); '"that pride alone could have moved the marshal to have the fortress stormed with such fury in the circumstances, namely to increase his glory by taking it by force of arms"' (OCR); Victoires, as in claims victoires-side-b and victoires-side-a.

claims.value: Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne commanded at Scharnitz under Archduke John, who told him that holding the fortress for at least three more days was necessary and charged him not to begin the retreat without a definite order. In Moriggl's OCR, Swinburne refused Ney's written and oral summonses; when the turning columns appeared he sent a company of soldiers to the Landesvertheidiger on each side and asked FML Count St. Julien at Innsbruck to replace them, and when the fighting ended he asked Seefeld for men for the next day. He had the Landesvertheidiger defend the Arnthal and the Arnthalkopf to the left of the fortress, and the garrison, spurred on by him, beat off three general assaults. Late in the evening, on certain news that the enemy was already in Seefeld, the Landesvertheidiger were told to find their own way out; Swinburne took one gun, had the other eleven spiked, gathered his men and marched toward Seefeld, intending to break through and join Archduke John's army corps. Pushed off the road toward the mountain by the French column on the Geigenbichl, attacked in his right flank by a second detachment from Seefeld and forestalled at the defile of the rothe Kreuz by a third, he surrendered with his men after a short but vigorous attempt to force the passage.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions at Scharnitz as Moriggl gives them (page images except where marked OCR). Victoires names no Austrian commander; its Austrian chief was unhorsed and taken by Captain Genevay (claim bodart-winner). In Moriggl's OCR the Archduke, before leaving Innsbruck, also left St. Julien a written instruction to have Swinburne and Kraus withdraw in the night to Innsbruck once the troops of Chasteler and Rohan had passed (claim side-b-objectives); the passages read do not say whether that order reached Swinburne. English renderings (ours): 'the Archduke further declared to him that holding the fortress for at least three more days was necessary, and charged him not to begin the retreat without a definite order for it'; 'I am, however, with all the troops under my command firmly resolved to defend the post entrusted to me, as befits brave soldiers' (OCR); '"he who does his duty has nothing to reproach himself with", said Swinburne, "adieu!"' (OCR); as in claim moriggl-side-a for the turning columns; 'when Swinburne noticed this, he quickly sent the Landesvertheidiger left and right a company of soldiers in support and a courier to Innsbruck, asking FML Count St. Julien for the speedy replacement of the ... (OCR) companies gone to the threatened points' (OCR); 'in which Swinburne ordered the alarm to be beaten and good numbers of men sent into Scharnitz, of whom he (as he believed) would need a great many more for the following day' (OCR); 'earlier he had urgently asked FML Count St. Julien for support in men and more guns' (OCR); 'these, by the commandant's instruction, had to defend the Arnthal and the Arnthalkopf to the left of the fortress'; 'three general assaults were in this way happily beaten off by the brave garrison; spurred on by its commandant, it worked wonders of bravery on this hot day and covered itself with glory'; 'for when Swinburne had received late in the evening the certain news that the enemy was already in Seefeld, the Landesvertheidiger were given the instruction to seek a way out for themselves'; 'but so he took one gun, had the other eleven spiked, gathered his men and marched bravely at their head toward Seefeld'; '[with] one gun was on the march, with the intention of breaking through and joining the army corps of Archduke John'; 'he was pushed by the French column that held the Geigenbichl at once off the road and toward the mountain'; 'but a second French detachment broke out of Seefeld at the same time and fell on his right flank, while a third enemy detachment advanced quickly on the road and reached the "rothe' (p. 363) 'Kreuz" before Swinburne and occupied the defile' (p. 364); 'thus surrounded on all sides, the brave warrior had to surrender with his brave men (truly worthy of a better lot) to the overwhelming enemy, after a short but vigorous attempt to force the passage'.

claims.value: Major Kraus commanded the Kinsky battalion and the Leutasch fort. Having taken command on 28 October, he asked the inhabitants which posts were most dangerous and was told that the Alpl was the most dangerous point, and he was often reminded that it had to be well held because the enemy would almost certainly try to break in there; Moriggl says he did nothing to strengthen it, though he had 7 days and 900 men, and posted 24 soldiers with an officer on the Alpl and 14 militiamen on the Grünkopf. A deputation of Leutasch men, taken by the governor to Archduke John to obtain an order to Kraus to hold the Alpl more strongly, was not heeded. In Moriggl's OCR, on 4 November Kraus refused the Alpl post's request for men and ammunition and Captain Sailer's requests to go to its help; when the French appeared on the height he withdrew toward Oberleutasch with a gun, and Captain Baron Horn took command in the work and sent companies to the Alpl, too late. An imperial officer then told the militia to get away, since the soldiers would have to surrender; Captain Sailer fought on with the soldiers and was taken. Horn made some weak attempts to hold the place, which was already surrounded; after two French officers told him that a column of over 3000 men stood in the rear of the work and that all the Landesvertheidiger had been pushed back, a capitulation was concluded.
claims.rationale: The Leutasch decisions as Moriggl gives them (page images except where marked OCR). By his own statement his narrative of the Leutasch is taken mainly from the protocol of eyewitness statements that the Tyrolean government and estates had taken and published (OCR). Judgments, not recorded facts: Moriggl calls Kraus's refusal of help wholly unforgivable; the published protocol says the poor occupation of the Alpl cannot be laid to the militia, whose wish to send help was always rejected with contempt; and he quotes a staff officer, author of a work on Archduke John's army of 1809, that the utter neglect of the flank position in the Leutasch by Major Kraus decided the loss of the Tyrol (all OCR). English renderings (ours): as in claim moriggl-leutasch for Kraus's command and his posts; 'hardly had Major Kraus received the command in the Leutasch on 28 October when he inquired urgently of the inhabitants which were the most dangerous posts'; 'but that the Alpl was the most dangerous point of all'; 'Major Kraus was afterwards reminded still more often that the Alpl had to be very well occupied, because the enemy would almost' (p. 339) 'certainly try to break in from that side, since he would not come directly at the work' (p. 340); 'they decided to send a deputation to Archduke John at Innsbruck, to draw his attention to the importance of the post and to bring about an order to Major Kraus to occupy the "Alpl" more strongly'; 'the deputies were taken at once by the governor, who recognized the importance of their request, to the Archduke, but by him were not heeded, and by his adjutants even turned away with scorn'; 'so the fateful fourth of November had come'; '[he] hurried down the mountain as orderly to report the enemy's approach to the commandant in the work and at the same time to ask him to send more men and also ammunition up in support of the post on the Alpl' (OCR); '"let them come," Kraus replied, "there are soldiers up there already, and here the pieces are laid"' (OCR); 'the weak party up there remained without support' (OCR); 'Captain Sailer had the commandant asked in this matter' (OCR); '"whether he might not come to the help of the post on the Alpl? Every man of his company wished to receive leave for it"' (OCR); '"the company stays where it is; let no one leave his post"' (OCR); 'that, as danger approached, he refused the good people up there the urgently requested help, indeed stubbornly and obstinately denied it, one might say is wholly unforgivable and irresponsible' (OCR); 'suddenly the ... (OCR) French come into view on the height' (OCR); 'there Major Kraus withdraws with a gun toward Oberleutasch!' (OCR); 'in place of the departed Major the eldest captain, Baron Horn, now took over the command in the work' (OCR); 'he at once (but unfortunately already too late) sent ... (OCR) companies off to the Alpl' (OCR); '"peasants, now take yourselves off; we cannot answer for you. As for us soldiers, we must surrender"'; 'he fought on beside the military as long as the fight lasted at all, was taken prisoner with the imperial soldiers and led away with them to France'; 'Captain Baron Horn indeed made some weak attempts to hold the place; but it was already completely surrounded by the enemy'; 'then two French officers appeared before the work with a drummer and asked to speak with the commandant'; as in claim moriggl-side-a for the column of over 3000; 'further informed him that all the Landesvertheidiger had been pushed back, so that he had no help to expect, etc., the following capitulation was concluded'; '[the narrative] itself is taken in the main from the protocol that the united provincial government and estates later took with some Landesvertheidiger who were eyewitnesses of the whole event' (OCR); 'that the poor occupation of this post, namely the Alpl, which with only a somewhat larger number of defenders would have been unclimbable, can truly not be laid to the charge of the militia' (OCR); 'rather the best will of the same to send help there was always rejected with contempt, to the general discontent and loud grumbling of the men' (OCR); 'the utter neglect of the flank position in the Leutasch by Major' (p. 352) 'Kraus against Generals Loison and Labassée decided the loss of the Tyrol' (p. 353, OCR).

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) under Marshal Ney over side B (Austrian) under Lieutenant-Colonel Swinburne. In Moriggl the garrison of Scharnitz beat off three general assaults and the French withdrew to Mittenwald for the night, but the Leutasch work capitulated to Loison's column the same day, Swinburne's column surrendered near Seefeld, and Ney entered the abandoned fortress. In Victoires the 69th escaladed the fort, and the Austrian troop that had evacuated it, caught between two fires near a monastery and deprived of its chief, laid down its arms; Ney was then master of the Pass of Scharnitz.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending, read from the page images. No source read gives a different result. The accounts differ on how the fort was taken (claims side-a-command and victoires-side-a): Moriggl has three assaults beaten off on 4 November and the garrison leave, with Ney entering the abandoned fortress toward 4 in the morning; Victoires mentions no assault on the 4th and has the 69th escalade the fort on 5 November under fire from its ramparts. Moriggl records praise of the defence from side A: French officers described the assaults to Dipauli as the most stubborn they had seen, and Stabenrath certified that Swinburne and Major de la Lippe had won Ney's esteem by their brilliant defence of the fort. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Moriggl, as in claim side-b-command for the assaults and the surrender; 'at ¼ past 5 in the evening the last cannon shot from Scharnitz was heard up in Seefeld; the French withdrew to Mittenwald'; 'in consequence of this capitulation the whole imperial garrison was led away as prisoners of war over the Burberg to Mittenwald and shut up there in the church'; as in claim side-a-command for Ney's entry; 'for, as Herr von Dipauli expressly remarks, several French officers described to him the assaults on Scharnitz as the most stubborn they had ever seen'; '[is owed] to Herr Swinburne, lieutenant-colonel, and Herr de la Lippe, major, and that these two staff officers knew how to earn the esteem of Marshal Ney by their brilliant defence of the fort of Scharnitz to such a degree'; Victoires, as in claim victoires-side-a for the columns of 5 November and the combat near the monastery, as in claim scharnitz-ground for the escalade and as in claim victoires-side-b for the evacuation; 'the Austrian troop, caught between two fires, lost all its advantage; surrounded on all sides and deprived of its chief, unhorsed and taken prisoner by Captain Genevay, it was forced to lay down its arms and submit to the law of the victor'; 'master of the Pass of Scharnitz, Marshal Ney hastened the march of his troops on Innsbruck'.

claims.value: Side A's loss in the other accounts. Moriggl calls the statements of French dead and wounded at Scharnitz remarkably various: a French report says the whole undertaking cost the French about 36 dead and about 400 wounded, most of whom only had their wounds dressed and then followed the army; another enemy report says the day cost the victors several hundred dead and wounded; the military Zeitschrift and the Sammler give the loss as 800 men; and a total loss of 1800 men is often found, a figure he says cannot be proved, though the loss must in any case have been great. By the diary he often cites, the French dragged many dead into barns between Mittenwald and Scharnitz, which were then burned with the fallen. At the Leutasch the French counted, by their own statement, 10 dead and 6 wounded. Victoires gives no figure in the passages read.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images and not combined; Moriggl does not name the two French reports. In his OCR he also calls wrong the Sammler's statement that Ney had already stormed the fortress the day before and lost men there (date and number not restated). English renderings (ours): 'remarkable is the varying statement of the French killed and wounded'; 'whereas a French report on the loss suffered on this hot day expresses itself thus:'; '"the whole undertaking cost the French about 36 dead and about 400 wounded, most of whom only had themselves bandaged and then followed the army"'; 'another enemy report expresses itself as follows:'; '"this day cost the victors (namely the French) several hundred dead and wounded"'; 'the military Zeitschrift and the "Sammler" give the loss as 800 men'; 'the enemy's total loss is often found given as 1800 men, a figure, however, that cannot be proved; it must in any case have been great'; 'according to the diary often cited, the French had dragged many dead into the barns that stood on the meadows between' (p. 335) 'Mittenwald and Scharnitz; these were then set on fire together with the fallen, who lay over one another like "logs", and given to the flames' (p. 336); 'as for the loss suffered on both sides, the French counted by their own statement 10 dead and 6 wounded'; 'it is therefore an error when one reads in the Sammler that Ney had already on ... (OCR) November made an assault on the fortress and lost ... (OCR) men in it' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B's loss in the other accounts. Moriggl: at Scharnitz the Austrians, well covered in the works, had no more than sixteen dead (11 in the Vorschanzl, 2 between it and the first battery, 2 in the first battery and 1 in the village, by an eyewitness who helped bury them); the number of wounded is unknown, among them the battalion adjutant Karl von Ehrenstein and the artillery first lieutenant Frisch, who died at Innsbruck; of the Landesvertheidiger only one dead is known there, Joseph Fechtl of Seefeld, though more may have fallen. At the Leutasch the capitulation made the garrison prisoners of war, the officers released on their word until exchanged and all munitions and arms in the fort to belong to France, and the whole imperial garrison was taken to Mittenwald; 12 men and 1 officer of the imperial troops were killed, and the Tyroleans had 2 officers dead and several men wounded. The Landesvertheidiger's dead of 4 November totalled nine, Fechtl among them; the Sammler's 90 is right, he says, if the nought is left off. At Seefeld nine imperial soldiers were killed and many wounded, an officer among them; with two dragoons killed the day before, eleven imperial soldiers fell in and around Seefeld and were buried in one grave with six murdered Landesvertheidiger. Swinburne surrendered with his men, having taken one gun and spiked the other eleven; an officer, some artillerymen and a few soldiers had gone off with the Landesvertheidiger to headquarters at Steinach. Stabenrath's certificate, which Moriggl quotes, has him escort a detachment of 1000 Austrian prisoners of war from Innsbruck to Kufstein, including 16 officers of the Scharnitz garrison. Victoires: three hundred men capitulated at the Leutasch, and eighteen hundred men, a flag and sixteen guns with their teams were the immediate result of the day.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images and not combined. Moriggl gives no total of prisoners; Victoires's eighteen hundred and Bodart's about 1,500 mostly prisoners (claim bodart-losses) are not in his passages, and Stabenrath's 1000 were one detachment, not necessarily every prisoner. Fechtl, the one Landesvertheidiger dead Moriggl knows at Scharnitz, is among the nine of 4 November, so the nine cover both posts. Moriggl's eleven spiked guns and one taken along account for his 12 at Scharnitz; Victoires's sixteen guns with their teams taken at Scharnitz do not fit that account, and the passages read do not say whether Bodart's 16 include the Leutasch pieces. English renderings (ours): Moriggl, 'as for the loss on the side of the Austrians, who were excellently covered in the works, they had no more than sixteen dead'; 'of these 11 lay in the Vorschanzl, 2 between it and the first battery, 2 in the first battery and 1 in the village, by the assurance of an eyewitness who helped bury them'; 'among the wounded, whose number is unknown, was also the battalion adjutant Karl von Ehrenstein', 'as well as the artillery first lieutenant Frisch'; 'where he died in the very first night after his arrival'; 'on the side of the Landesvertheidiger only one dead is known, namely Joseph Fechtl of Seefeld; it is possible, however, that more fell'; '1. The Austrian garrison are prisoners of war and lay down their arms; the officer, however, keeps his baggage and the private what he has in his knapsack'; '2. The officers are released on their word of honour until exchanged'; '3. To France shall belong everything in munitions and arms that is in the fort'; as in claim bodart-winner for the garrison led away; 'of the imperial military 12 privates and 1 officer were killed'; 'the Tyroleans had 2 officers dead and several privates wounded'; 'altogether the total loss of the Landesvertheidiger on 4 November in dead came to the following nine men'; 'from Seefeld (Jos. Fechtl) | 1'; 'together | 9 men'; 'in the Sammler the total loss is given as 90 men, quite right if the nought is left off'; 'nine imperial soldiers remained dead on the spot in this action; many were wounded, among them also an officer'; 'with those two dragoons who had fallen (the day before), the number of imperial soldiers fallen in and around Seefeld came to eleven men, who with the six murdered Landesvertheidiger all found their rest in one grave in the churchyard'; as in claim side-b-command for the surrender and the guns; 'an officer, some artillerymen with a few soldiers had joined them, came safely to Hall and from there over the Ellbögen to headquarters at Steinach'; Stabenrath, 'charged to lead a detachment of 1000 Austrian prisoners of war from Innsbruck to Kufstein'; 'that the marshal of the Empire left them their arms, as also to the 16 officers of the same garrison of Scharnitz who form part of the detachment'; Victoires, as in claim victoires-side-b for the three hundred; 'eighteen hundred men, a flag and sixteen pieces of cannon with their teams were the immediate result of this day'.

claims.value: Bodart places Scharnitz, a market town in the Tyrol, on the Isar 15 km north-west of Innsbruck. In Moriggl the fortress had a forward work (the Vorschanzl), batteries and works on the Kapfelberg; the rock walls of the steep Brunnstein rose on its right, where Grueber's riflemen prepared stone batteries, and the Arnthal and Arnthalkopf lay to its left, through which, he says in the OCR, the fortress could have been turned at close range. The Leutasch work had a wall running steeply toward the Grünkopf on its left and wooden steps on its right, and the military held its works in the plain; in the OCR its holding depended on points around it, the most dangerous being the Alpl, reached from Bavaria by a smugglers' path on which a passage only a few feet wide was left unoccupied. The road rises considerably from Scharnitz to Unterseefeld, and the French blocked Swinburne at the defile of the rothe Kreuz near Seefeld. Victoires has the fort on a plateau reached by escalading sheer rocks several hundred feet high, and Seefeld a village in front of the Pass of Scharnitz.
claims.rationale: Ground from Bodart's location and the two accounts, read from the page images except where marked OCR; no map was inspected. The passages read do not give, from a page image, how far the Leutasch work lies from Scharnitz. Moriggl's OCR has a Kloster at Seefeld where Loison lodged; the passages read do not say it is Victoires's monastery on the road. claims.value: Archduke John granted each man at Scharnitz daily half a pound of meat and half a Seitel of brandy, the supply assigned to the postmaster at Zirl, Anton Niederkircher. The fortress had only 12 guns where 50 could easily have been used, and the Leutasch work three guns and a howitzer. In Moriggl's OCR, Major von Leiß wrote that before the reinforcement the garrison had been too weak to man the line and had no reserve; Swinburne had poles with iron hooks prepared, with which the scaling ladders were thrown down; at the Leutasch the Alpl post asked for men and ammunition, and Kraus's advance with the Landsturm ended when the ammunition ran out. Side A's turning column took carriers requisitioned at Mittenwald (OCR), and in Victoires the 69th climbed with their knapsacks tied on their heads against the balls and stones.

claims.value: In Moriggl's OCR, Ney reconnoitred the fortress and the Leutasch valley with his staff and some men who knew the area; Loison's turning column had reliable guides, the Bavarian forest warden Anton Wurmer, a native of Mittenwald who knew the area well, and the Bavarian district forester Johann Trysberger of Krün; the postmaster of Mittenwald was suspected of having led the whole turning movement; and Moriggl judges that the French must have been well informed of the weak occupation of the Alpl. At the Leutasch French officers told Horn that a column of over 3000 men stood in the rear of the work and that all the Landesvertheidiger had been pushed back. In the night of 4 to 5 November Ney received at Mittenwald, it was said through a deserter, the news that the Scharnitz garrison had already left.

claims.value: In Moriggl's OCR, side B was warned of the threat through the Leutasch: Major von Leiß wrote to Innsbruck that he feared greatly for the Leutasch, and the defence deputation wrote that Scharnitz could very easily be turned from there. Kraus was told by the inhabitants that the Alpl was the most dangerous point and was often reminded to hold it well, and a deputation to Archduke John on the point was not heeded. On 4 November the militia posted on the Grünkopf saw the French coming from a considerable distance, and their messenger reported it to Kraus, who dismissed it (OCR). After the assault Swinburne did not yet know how badly things stood in the Leutasch (OCR); late in the evening he received certain news that the enemy was already in Seefeld. The Tyrolean Jäger that St. Julien sent toward Scharnitz met the enemy in Seefeld and turned back (OCR).

claims.value: Napoleon had directed Marshal Ney with his army corps to invade the Tyrol and seize it, and the marshal wanted to attack the Pass of Scharnitz (Victoires). In Moriggl, Loison's task was to turn the Leutasch work, take it and then take the fortress of Scharnitz in the rear.
claims.rationale: Aims as the accounts give them, read from the page images. The aim of invading the Tyrol was set by Napoleon's order, so the claim is tagged inherited; the plan of attack was Ney's (claims side-a-command and posture). Ney's written summons set a limit on how long a refusal would hold up his march (OCR; the period, a number word, is not restated), and Moriggl's judgment on Ney's motive is recorded in claim side-a-command. claims.value: Side B's task was set from above. Swinburne had reported that he and his garrison were resolved to repel every attack and every proposal of surrender and would leave the post only after the utmost resistance and only as he had been ordered (the first part OCR); Archduke John answered that holding the fortress for at least three more days was necessary and charged him not to begin the retreat without a definite order. In Moriggl's OCR, the written instruction the Archduke left with St. Julien was to secure the Leutasch and Scharnitz as long as possible, so that at least the troops of Chasteler and Rohan had time to reach the Brenner, and then to send Swinburne and Major Kraus the order to withdraw from their posts in the night and march to Innsbruck. claims.value: Side A attacked. In Moriggl, Ney decided after Swinburne's refusal to take the place by force (OCR); on 4 November his troops stormed the fortress from 1 o'clock to ¼ past 5 in three general assaults, which were beaten off, while Loison's column turned and took the Leutasch work; after Loison reached Seefeld, French detachments pushed Swinburne's withdrawing column off the road, fell on its flank and forestalled it at the defile, where it surrendered after a short attempt to force the passage. claims.value: Side B fought from works. Moriggl's Scharnitz is a fortress whose garrison, well covered in the works, beat off the assaults, with Landesvertheidiger in the works, especially on the Kapfelberg; in his OCR the assaulting columns set ladders against the works. The Leutasch work, also called a fort, had a wall toward the Grünkopf and works in the plain held by the military. claims.rationale: Code B_fortified: both accounts have side B defend the fortress of Scharnitz and the Leutasch work, permanent works in place before the campaign. open_questions: Deferred: Moriggl's text between the selected sections at pp. 300-302, 323-330 and 353-362, read in the OCR while locating the passages and not cited (the Archduke's orders of the morning of 4 November, the Innsbruck defence deputation's measures, and the French entry into Seefeld and the night that followed); the sources Moriggl uses but which were not inspected (Swinburne's papers, the Seefeld diary, Dipauli's notes and the published protocol of eyewitness statements on the Leutasch); the unnamed French reports and the Oesterreichische militärische Zeitschrift he quotes for side A's loss; any report of Ney or Loison and the bulletins of the Grande Armée, which the passages read do not cite; the rest of Moriggl's order of battle (pp. 89-94: the other corps, the cavalry reserve, the Guard, the recapitulation, which repeats the VI Corps' total, and the troops that arrived later), read from the page images except p. 91, read in the OCR, and not cited. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the number of guns sent with the Erzherzog Karl battalion; the ordinal of the day of Ney's reconnaissance and of Dupont's division; the number of corps in Ney's summons and the day by which he said a refusal would delay him; the date and loss in the Sammler's statement that Moriggl corrects; the number of outworks given to Marcognet's brigade, of Villatte's turning columns and their ordinals, and of companies Swinburne asked to have replaced; the hour at which he did not yet know the Leutasch's fate; the number of companies of Tyrolean Jäger St. Julien sent; the strength of Seeger's Landsturm column; the number of the Leutasch work's bastions, the year on its beam, and the number and ordinal of the points it depended on; the number of companies Horn sent to the Alpl; the ordinal in the militia's sighting of the French; the page numbers of the parent, read from the OCR except where a page image is cited.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength. Neither Moriggl nor Victoires gives a total for the action; Bodart's about 13,000 is not in the passages read, and Moriggl's 3000 for Labassée's brigade is his narrative's only figure for part of it. The targeted follow-up, Moriggl's order of battle of the Grande Armée at its crossing of the Rhine (pp. 89 and 92, transcribed from the page images), gives Ney's corps by division (claim moriggl-order-of-battle): Loison's and Malcher's divisions, whose brigades the narrative engages at the two posts, had 15,615 men together at the crossing (our sum). That narrows the gap without closing it, since the crossing comes before Elchingen and Ulm in Moriggl's narrative and in his OCR Ney left a considerable part of his forces at Ulm. A return of Ney's corps for early November or a report of Ney or Loison, none of which the passages read cite, could close it. Side B's prisoners are uncertain too: Moriggl gives each post's garrison but no count of prisoners, and Victoires's 1,800 and Bodart's about 1,500 have no stated basis.

Disputes recorded in the claims: how the fort fell (Moriggl: three assaults beaten off on 4 November, the garrison's departure in the night and Ney's entry into the abandoned fortress toward 4 in the morning; Victoires: no assault on the 4th, and the 69th escalading the fort under fire on 5 November and finding about a hundred Tyrolean chasseurs); the Leutasch garrison (Victoires three hundred; Moriggl a battalion given as 600 with militia companies of 117 and 219); side B's prisoners and trophies (Victoires eighteen hundred men, a flag and sixteen guns with their teams; Bodart about 1,500 mostly prisoners, 16 guns and 1 flag; Moriggl no total, twelve guns at Scharnitz of which eleven were spiked, and a detachment of 1000 prisoners escorted to Kufstein); side A's loss (Bodart about 400; the reports Moriggl quotes give about 36 dead and about 400 wounded, several hundred, 800 and 1800; and 10 dead and 6 wounded at the Leutasch); the date of the fort's fall, 5 November in Victoires against Bodart's 4 November for the engagement.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 16 guns equal Moriggl's twelve at Scharnitz and four pieces at the Leutasch together and Victoires's sixteen, and his 400 for side A equals the wounded in a French report Moriggl quotes; his strengths are not in the passages read); Moriggl (the Tyrolean account of 1861, an interested one, written from Swinburne's papers, the Seefeld diary, Dipauli's notes, the published eyewitness protocol and his own interviews; he quotes unnamed French reports and the Oesterreichische militärische Zeitschrift for side A's loss, and names no source for his order of battle at the Rhine crossing); Victoires et conquêtes (the French compilation of 1819, an interested one, which names no sources in the passages read and may draw on the bulletins, not checked).
